auslegerkanu#definition: A canoe with a float, the outrigger, attached to the side of the hull to stabilize it against capsizing. To settle the Pacific, voyagers also used large double-hulled canoes with sails of pandanus matting that could carry people, animals and plants across thousands of kilometres. They navigated without instruments by the stars, ocean swells, clouds and the flight of birds.
baray#definition: Khmer term for the great rectangular reservoirs built by the kings of Angkor; the West Baray measures about eight by two kilometres. They served the water supply and at the same time had religious meaning as an image of the primordial ocean around the cosmic mountain Meru. How much they contributed to irrigating the rice fields is judged differently by scholars.
basileus#definition: The Greek word for "king", which from the time of Emperor Heraclius served officially as the title of the Byzantine emperor. The basileus saw himself as the successor of the Roman emperors and as the God-appointed ruler of Christendom. Byzantium recognized the claim of Western rulers such as Charlemagne to the imperial title only reluctantly.
bilderstreit#definition: The conflict in Byzantium between about 726/730 and 843 over whether religious images may be venerated. The iconoclasts ("image-breakers") rejected this as idolatry, while the iconophiles ("image-lovers") defended it. After two phases of hostility to images, their veneration was finally restored in 843; since most sources come from the victors, the extent of the persecutions is disputed.
bojaren#definition: The noble upper class in Kievan Rus, in the Muscovite state and in the Danubian principalities. They owned large estates, advised the prince in the boyar duma and held high offices in the army and administration. Ivan IV persecuted them in the oprichnina, and Peter the Great abolished the rank and replaced it with the Table of Ranks.
danegeld#definition: Tribute payments with which English and Frankish rulers induced Viking armies to withdraw or sought to avert attacks. In England King Æthelred paid ever larger sums in silver from 991 onward, collected as a tax from the whole country. The payments made raiding profitable and explain the many English coins in Scandinavian hoards.
danelag#definition: The area in the north and east of England that was settled by Scandinavians in the late 9th century and in which Danish law applied. The name came into use only in the 11th century. Place names ending in -by and -thorpe and Scandinavian loanwords such as “sky” or “egg” still recall it today.
devaraja#definition: Sanskrit for "god-king"; the name of a royal cult introduced in the Khmer Empire by Jayavarman II in 802. It closely linked the king's rule with a deity, usually Shiva, and was maintained by a priestly family. What exactly the cult meant, and whether the king himself was regarded as a god, is disputed among scholars.
edda#definition: The name of two Icelandic works of the 13th century, the most important source for Norse mythology. Snorri Sturluson’s Prose Edda is a handbook of poetry that retells the myths of the gods; the Poetic Edda is a collection of older poems about gods and heroes. Since both were written down by Christians, it is debated how faithfully they reflect pre-Christian belief.
gewuerzinseln#definition: An island group in the east of present-day Indonesia, for a long time the only place in the world where cloves grew; nutmeg came only from the nearby Banda Islands. The desire to control this trade drove the Portuguese, Spanish, English and Dutch to Southeast Asia. In the 17th century the Dutch East India Company imposed a monopoly with great violence.
griechisches-feuer#definition: An incendiary weapon that the Byzantine navy sprayed from tubes at enemy ships from the 7th century and that kept burning even on water. Its composition was a closely guarded state secret and is still not known for certain; it probably contained petroleum. It played a decisive part in repelling the Arab sieges of Constantinople.
ikone#definition: An image of Christ, Mary or a saint, usually painted on wood, that is venerated in the Orthodox Church. According to Orthodox teaching the veneration is directed not at the image itself but at the person depicted; the icon is understood as a window onto the heavenly world. The legitimacy of this veneration was fought over in the Iconoclast controversy of the 8th and 9th centuries.
jarl#definition: A high Scandinavian noble title denoting a powerful chieftain or a governor on behalf of the king. In the 10th century the jarls of Lade ruled large parts of Norway, and the jarls of Orkney governed the islands north of Scotland. The English noble title “earl” is related to the word and took on its meaning under Cnut the Great.
katipunan#definition: A secret society founded by Andrés Bonifacio in Manila in 1892 to win the independence of the Philippines from Spain by force of arms. Its name is short for a Tagalog title meaning roughly "Supreme and Most Venerable Society of the Children of the Nation". Its discovery in August 1896 marked the start of the Philippine Revolution.
kosaken#definition: Free, militarily organized communities in the steppes of present-day Ukraine and southern Russia that emerged from the 15th century onwards from runaway peasants and adventurers. They elected their own leaders, the atamans or hetmans, and served Polish kings and tsars as border troops. At the same time they led great uprisings and carried the conquest of Siberia.
kultursystem#definition: Dutch "cultuurstelsel"; the system of forced cultivation introduced on Java in 1830. Villages had to use part of their land or labour for export crops such as coffee, sugar and indigo, which the colonial state bought at low prices. It brought the Netherlands large profits but caused hardship and famine on Java, and it was gradually abolished from 1870.
kyrillische-schrift#definition: A writing system for Slavic languages developed from the Greek alphabet, which arose in the late 9th and early 10th centuries among the disciples of Cyril and Methodius in the Bulgarian Empire and is named after Cyril. Cyril himself had earlier created the Glagolitic script. Today Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Bulgarian, Serbian and Macedonian, among others, are written in Cyrillic.
langschiff#definition: The slender warship of the Vikings, clinker-built from overlapping planks, with a keel, square sail and rowing benches. It was seaworthy and had so shallow a draught that it could penetrate far up rivers and land on flat beaches. Finds such as the Gokstad and Skuldelev ships show lengths of about 20 to 30 metres.
lapita-kultur#definition: An archaeological culture, named after a site in New Caledonia, that appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago in the second half of the 2nd millennium BC. Its hallmark is pottery with finely stamped geometric patterns. Its bearers spoke Austronesian languages, settled the islands as far as Tonga and Samoa within a few centuries and are regarded as the ancestors of the Polynesians.
leibeigenschaft#definition: The legal binding of peasants to the land and to a lord, to whom they owed labour and dues. In Russia it was tightened from the late 16th century and made hereditary in 1649; serfs could be sold and handed over to the army. Alexander II abolished it in 1861; in the Baltic provinces it had already ended between 1816 and 1819.
mana#definition: A Polynesian term for a supernatural power, authority and prestige that people, ancestors, places and objects can possess. Chiefs and kings derived their mana from divine ancestors; success in war increased it, while defeats or breaches of tapu could diminish it. The concept still plays a major role in Polynesian cultures today.
mandala-staat#definition: A model historians use to describe the early states of Southeast Asia: a centre of power was surrounded by circles of dependent princes and ports whose loyalty depended on the strength and prestige of the ruler. Borders were vague, and the same territories could pay tribute to several centres at once. The concept explains why kingdoms such as Srivijaya or Majapahit could grow and shrink so quickly.
moai#definition: The large stone figures of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), of which almost 900 are known. They represent ancestors and mostly stood on ceremonial platforms, the ahu, facing inland. Most were carved from tuff in the Rano Raraku crater; some bore topknots of red scoria, the pukao.
orthodoxe-kirche#definition: The communion of Eastern churches that grew out of the imperial church of Byzantium; "orthodox" means "right-believing". It consists of self-governing national churches, among which the patriarch of Constantinople holds a primacy of honour, and it does not recognize the pope as its head. Its hallmarks include the liturgy in traditional church languages such as Greek and Church Slavonic rather than Latin, the veneration of icons and a strong monastic tradition.
pa-festung#definition: A fortified Māori settlement, usually on a hill, ridge or headland and protected by ditches, earth banks and palisades. Many thousands of pā have been identified archaeologically; they secured villages and food stores in times of conflict. In the New Zealand Wars, Māori built pā with trenches and bunkers that withstood British artillery fire remarkably well.
runen#definition: The written characters of the Germanic peoples, carved mainly into stone, wood and metal. The older runic row, called the futhark after its first characters, had 24 signs; in the Viking Age a younger row with 16 signs was in use in Scandinavia. Most of the surviving runestones stand in Sweden and commemorate the dead or journeys abroad.
saga#definition: A prose narrative in Old Norse, of the kind written down above all in Iceland in the 13th and 14th centuries. The sagas of Icelanders tell of families of the settlement period, their feuds and voyages, while the kings’ sagas deal with the rulers of Norway. They are based on oral tradition but were composed generations after the events and must therefore be used with caution as historical sources.
semstwo#definition: An elected body of rural self-government that Alexander II introduced in 1864 at the level of provinces and districts. The zemstvos maintained schools, hospitals and roads and employed doctors, teachers and agronomists. They became a rallying point for liberal forces demanding a constitution.
solidus#definition: The gold coin introduced by Constantine the Great in the early 4th century, struck at 72 to a Roman pound of gold. Known in the Greek East as the nomisma, it kept its value until the 11th century and was a sought-after currency throughout the Mediterranean. After a period of debasement, Alexios I replaced it in 1092 with the hyperpyron.
szlachta#definition: The nobility of Poland-Lithuania, which was unusually numerous at an estimated six to ten per cent of the population and ranged from rich magnates to landless petty nobles. Its members were regarded as equal in law, elected the king from 1573 and dominated the parliament. Their "golden freedom" protected against royal arbitrariness but weakened the state.
tapu#definition: A Polynesian term for what is sacred and forbidden, from which the word "taboo" derives; in Hawaiʻi it is "kapu". Tapu rested on people, places and things connected with gods or mana, and anyone who violated it could expect misfortune or punishment. James Cook brought the word from Tonga to Europe.
terra-nullius#definition: Latin for "nobody's land": the legal notion that a territory belongs to no one and may therefore be taken without a treaty. The term itself came into use later, but it describes the basis of the British taking of Australia from 1788, in which Aboriginal land was annexed to the Crown without agreement or compensation. In 1992 the High Court of Australia rejected this assumption in the Mabo decision and recognized native title for the first time.
themenverfassung#definition: The military districts into which the Byzantine Empire was divided from the 7th century. Each was headed by a strategos who exercised both military and civil authority; the soldiers often came from the district itself. When and how this system arose, whether under Heraclius or gradually afterwards, is debated among historians.
theravada#definition: "Teaching of the Elders"; the branch of Buddhism based on the Pali Canon that places monastic life at its centre. It reached Southeast Asia mainly from Sri Lanka and from the 11th century became dominant in Pagan, later in Sukhothai, Ayutthaya, Laos and Cambodia. It remains the main religion of Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia today.
thing#definition: The assembly of free men in Germanic and Scandinavian societies, at which justice was administered, disputes settled and common matters decided. There were local things and large regional assemblies such as the Icelandic Althing or the Norwegian Gulating. The word lives on in the names of parliaments such as the Storting, Folketing and Alþingi.
traumzeit#definition: The usual English term for the world views of Aboriginal Australians, according to which ancestral beings created the landscape, living things, laws and customs in a time of creation. This time is not seen as a closed past but is present in places, songs, dances and ceremonies. It binds people to particular areas of country for which they are responsible; individual language groups have their own terms for it, such as "Jukurrpa" among the Warlpiri.
voc#definition: The United East India Company, founded in 1602, was a trading company with the Dutch monopoly on trade with Asia and the right to build forts, maintain soldiers and conclude treaties. From Batavia it dominated the spice trade and large parts of Java. It is regarded as one of the first joint-stock companies and was dissolved in 1799.
waraeger#definition: The East Slavic and Byzantine name for Scandinavian traders and warriors who travelled the river routes between the Baltic and the Black Sea in the 9th and 10th centuries. They played an important role in the emergence of Kievan Rus and served in Byzantium as the imperial bodyguard. How large their share in state formation was is disputed.
wetsche#definition: The assembly of free men in towns of the Rus, especially in Novgorod and Pskov. In Novgorod the veche elected the mayor and the archbishop, decided on war and peace and could summon and depose princes. It was abolished when Moscow subdued Novgorod in 1478.
zar#definition: A title of rulers derived from the Latin "Caesar", first borne in Russia by Ivan IV at his coronation in 1547. It put the ruler of Moscow on a level with the Byzantine emperor and emphasized his unlimited, God-given power. From 1721 the official title was emperor, but the term tsar remained in common use until 1917.
